title: The bard’s noserag! A new art colour for our Irish poets: snotgreen. You can almost taste it, can’t you?
html_source:
Mulligan’s epithet for Stephen—“the bard”—is both mocking and admiring: he acknowledges the young Dedalus’s talents as writer and poet while also suggesting that he acts above his station. “Bard” is a term most often attached to Shakespeare, but it also suggests a kind of travelling poet (appropriate for Joyce the exile) as well as a poet of national importance. Here, then, Mulligan suggests that Dedalus—and Joyce by extension—is, despite his youth and pretensions, a representative writer for Ireland with the weight of the country on his shoulders.

The colour green has long been highly symbolic in relation to Ireland. Mulligan’s compound “snotgreen” recalls—as noted below—Homer’s famous phrase “winedark sea”, tying Joyce to Homer as well as Shakespeare. The snot also evokes the candour Joyce habitually displayed when writing about bodily practices: snot will indeed play a role again, notably in the third chapter, “Proteus”. By suggesting that “snotgreen” might be “a new art colour for our Irish poets”, Mulligan also indicates some of the flavours and textures of modernist art, and the down-to-earthiness of Irish writers in particular. The handkerchief becomes a kind of canvas in this moment, with Stephen’s bodily effluence representing the art he has sent forth from himself.

It’s also appropriate that Mulligan would claim that this is a colour that “you can almost taste”.
